newsitem.title: USA: U.S. interest rate futures end lower, T-bonds lead.
newsitem.headline: U.S. interest rate futures end lower, T-bonds lead.

text.p: U.S. interest rate futures ended lower, with declines in T-bonds once again outstripping losses in Eurodollars.
With forecasts for a possible U.S. stock correction looming in the marketplace, investors' money flowed quietly into the short-end of the curve.
Seasonal profit-taking, meanwhile, continued to wrack U.S. bond futures, erasing any prospect for a near-term corrective bounce, traders said.
"Today would have been a good day to consolidate higher from Wednesday," one T-bond futures trader said.
"But it's pretty disappointing we couldn't get that going," he said, adding that March bond's break to 112-13/32, below 112-16/32, points to a decline to 112-04/32.

Traders and analysts are eyeing 112-08/32 as key support, as March tested that one-month low in reaction to Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's comments on "irrational exuberance" last Thursday evening.
Greenspan's comments have clouded the outlook for U.S. monetary policy, even though recent U.S. inflationary data suggests tepid price pressures and moderate economic growth.
"There is enough uncertainty out there," a trader said.
The 0.4-percent decline in U.S. November retail sales and the 0.3 percent increase in the overall Consumer Price Index (CPI) lifted March bonds above intraday resistance at 113-21/32.
However, the uncertainty on U.S. monetary policy encouraged light seasonal profit-taking, even as the U.S. dollar maintained a firm tone.

"This is all telling me that there are more people closing their books for the year," Kathy Jones, an analyst with Prudential Securities said. "It was a bad first half of the year and a good second half. They want to lock in profits."
Even though March bonds were trading about 10/32 to 13/32 lower at the end of the day, one floor trader said the market felt like it was trading about two points lower.
"It feels like a Friday market with everyone wanting to get out of their positions," he said.

He also noted that bond futures' open interest rose more than 14,000 contracts on Wednesday, indicating that investors and traders were loading up on short positions during the break to 112-24/32. Some traders speculated that foreign investors trapped by the illiquidity of high-yielding markets, like Canada, decided to sell U.S. positions.

"Regardless of who was doing the selling, it's typically bearish to see open interest and volume rising on down days," he said. Earlier in the week, when bonds rebounded slightly from Friday's lows, open interest was lower.
One prominent pit trader alone sold 2,000 March bonds from 112-17/32 to the daily low of 112-13/32. Order flow from retail firms was extremely light all day.

At the end of pit trade, March bonds were 13/32 lower at 112-16/32, 10-year notes were off 07/32 at 109-09/32, June T-bills were two bps lower at 94.87, March and June Eurodollars were steady at 94.44 and 94.30, respectively.
